name: Bilateral chewing habit

lead: The practice is to chew evenly on both sides of the mouth instead of favouring one. People do it hoping to keep the jaw muscles and face symmetrical, on the premise that one-sided chewing could contribute to facial asymmetry.

Chewing is mostly unconscious, though conscious input can influence it, and feedback from nerves in the teeth and jaw joints helps control how forcefully each muscle works. The pattern adapts to the food and to changes in the teeth. The link between chewing side and facial symmetry is a community theory, and no studies were found testing it.

paras: People simply switch sides as they eat, sometimes counting bites or alternating by mouthful, until it becomes habit. It costs nothing and is usually combined with other symmetry habits. Any change in face shape would be gradual, over months or years.
No documented harms were found for this practice. Tooth pain, missing teeth, jaw joint problems or dentures can change which side a person chews on, and a dentist can assess those.

angle.text: Users alternate the chewing side to load both jaw muscles evenly, hoping to keep the jaw and face shape balanced left to right. The link from chewing side to facial symmetry is a community theory, and no studies were found on it.

lead: The bilateral chewing habit is the practice of alternating the side used for chewing, usually in the hope of keeping the jaw muscles and the lower face even. People in looksmaxxing and jaw-focused circles adopt it because a strongly preferred chewing side is thought to build one masseter more than the other and to contribute to facial asymmetry, so chewing evenly is meant to keep the face balanced.

Chewing is mostly unconscious, but conscious input can influence it, and feedback from nerves in the teeth and jaw joints helps control how long and how forcefully each muscle acts.[1] The pattern of chewing adapts to the type of food and to changes in the teeth, such as tooth loss or dentures.[1]

No studies found linking habitual chewing side to facial asymmetry. Reference works attribute facial asymmetry to other factors, including slight offsets of the eyes, nose and mouth relative to the ear axis, asymmetric mouth movement in speech, prenatal and childhood influences and age-related soft-tissue change.[2]

paras: Mastication is controlled partly by sensory feedback from teeth and jaw joints, and the chewing pattern changes with food texture and dental status.[1]

Facial symmetry has been found to increase attractiveness ratings, with a larger effect for female faces, and symmetry and averageness contribute independently.[2] Reference works note that most people move the right side of the mouth more during speech and that asymmetry increases with age, so some natural left-right difference is typical.[2]
